{{Short description|Number theory concept}}
In number theory, a '''rational reciprocity law''' is a [[reciprocity law]] involving residue symbols that are related by a factor of +1 or –1 rather than a general root of unity.

As an example, there are rational [[Quartic reciprocity|biquadratic]] and [[octic reciprocity law]]s.  Define the symbol (''x''|''p'')<sub>''k''</sub> to be +1 if ''x'' is a ''k''-th power modulo the prime ''p'' and -1 otherwise.

Let ''p'' and ''q'' be distinct primes congruent to 1 modulo 4, such that (''p''|''q'')<sub>2</sub> = (''q''|''p'')<sub>2</sub> = +1.  Let ''p'' = ''a''<sup>2</sup> + ''b''<sup>2</sup> and ''q'' = ''A''<sup>2</sup> + ''B''<sup>2</sup> with ''aA'' odd.  Then

:<math> (p|q)_4 (q|p)_4 = (-1)^{(q-1)/4} (aB-bA|q)_2 \ . </math>

If in addition ''p'' and ''q'' are congruent to 1 modulo 8, let ''p'' = ''c''<sup>2</sup> + 2''d''<sup>2</sup> and ''q'' = ''C''<sup>2</sup> + 2''D''<sup>2</sup>.  Then

:<math> (p|q)_8 = (q|p)_8 = (aB-bA|q)_4 (cD-dC|q)_2 \ .</math>
